prize_parts.citation: For the conception and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, which led to the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson.

statement.case_for: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson is the clearest case on the shortlist of a concrete discovery that sits at the centre of the field. It completed the particle content of the Standard Model and gave empirical confirmation of electroweak symmetry breaking, which the 2013 prize honoured only on the theory side. It was independently established by two experiments, and the properties measured since (spin-parity, couplings) have held up. Fourteen years after the announcement, recognition of the experimental side is overdue. The key question is which people to name, and I think the founders and long-time leaders of the two experiments (Jenni for ATLAS, Della Negra and Virdee for CMS) are a defensible way to represent the two collaborations.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real and I do not want to hide it. The discovery was made by two collaborations of thousands, with machine builders, detector pioneers and the spokespersons at the moment of announcement all having claims, and any three-name set will be contested. Judged purely on opening support, B012 is not the front-runner: only one member ranked it first and four ranked it at all, and several colleagues clearly prefer cleaner single-idea cases. A committee that finds the credit allocation too arbitrary could reasonably prefer B029 or B031, where the discovery and the people line up much more neatly.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B029) are a clean measurement advance, with Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's record precision giving a tidy two-name credit, confirmed by many independent clocks and timely with the possible redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that B029 has the cleanest attribution on the list, and that is a genuine advantage over my own first choice. Where I differ is on weight. The clocks are a very fine achievement in precision measurement, but the redefinition of the second has not happened, and the test-of-fundamental-physics payoff is still mostly prospective. The Higgs is an actual discovery about nature. I would put B029 as a strong alternative and would not contest it vigorously, but I do not think a tidy credit assignment should outrank the importance of the finding.

responses.point: The gamma-ray burst afterglow discovery (B013) and IceCube (B037) are concrete observational discoveries, with B013 settling the cosmological origin of bursts and B037 founding neutrino astronomy, though IceCube is a large-collaboration effort with an attribution problem.
responses.response: We share a preference for discoveries over techniques, and I appreciate that you flagged the single-name problem for Halzen openly, since it is the same difficulty I have with B012. The comparison is instructive: the Higgs has two independent confirmations and a mature set of measurements, whereas for IceCube source identification is still developing and only partly confirmed by a second experiment. So I rank B012 above B037 on maturity. B013 is mature and well defined, but with a three-person credit that omits other BeppoSAX and follow-up contributors I do not see it as stronger than the Higgs on either importance or attribution.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B031) is an unusually clean theory-plus-experiment pairing that opened moire quantum matter, though the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated.
responses.response: B031 was my second choice because I find the pairing of the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction with the 2018 experiments compelling. I take your point about maturity seriously, and I would go further: the origin of the superconductivity and the correlated states is not settled, and early experimental co-authors such as Cao and Fatemi are outside the credited set. That makes me reluctant to put it first now. It remains my main alternative and, if the committee judges that the field has matured enough, I would back the three names Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.

responses.point: Trapped-ion quantum computing (B018) rests on the Cirac-Zoller proposal and Blatt's realisations, and is mature after three decades, but overlaps with the 2012 prize on single-quantum-system control.
responses.response: The 2012 overlap is for me the decisive qualification. Cirac and Zoller's proposal is conceptually important, but Wineland's prize already recognised control of individual ions, so the remaining increment is quantum computation as an application, whose practical impact is still unfolding. I would therefore leave B018 behind the discovery-based cases for now, though I accept the committee may see it differently.

uncertainties: Whether three names can fairly represent ATLAS and CMS, and whether spokespersons at the time of discovery, detector or accelerator pioneers should displace any of Jenni, Della Negra or Virdee; I rely on general knowledge of founding roles and have not verified them in detail.
Whether the committee would accept a prize for an experimental collaboration discovery given the credit problem, or prefer B029 on grounds of cleaner attribution.
Whether magic-angle graphene (B031) has matured enough, given the open question of the superconducting mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, early mentor Hector Rubinstein, frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group, and none of these is a credited name or an apparent collaborator of any shortlisted candidate.
